The Ten Perfections for Young (p. 1–15)

Pages 1–15 (15 pages)

The Ten Perfections for Young Readers From The Perfections Leading to Enlightenment by Sujin Boriharnwanaket, translated by Nina van Gorkom (Zolag, 2007) “May I, by this gift, enable beings to achieve long-life, beauty, happiness, strength, intelligence, and the supreme fruit of unsullied bliss.” Every Pali word is followed by its English in brackets. A quiz follows every two chapters; the answers are at the back. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 1

Page 3

How to read this book This book is about ten good qualities that the Buddha built up over many, many lives before he became the Buddha. They are called the ten pāramī (perfections). Each chapter takes one of them, explains it in plain words, and tells a true story from the Buddha’s past lives to show it in action. Pali words. The Buddha’s teaching was written down in a language called Pali. You will meet Pali words all through this book. Every time one appears, its English meaning sits right next to it in brackets, like this: dāna (giving), citta (mind). You never have to remember a Pali word to understand the page. But if you do remember a few, you will be able to read the ancient texts one day. Saying the words. A line over a letter makes it long: ā sounds like the “a” in “father”, ī like the “ee” in “see”, ū like the “oo” in “moon”. A dot under a letter (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) means you curl your tongue back a little. ñ sounds like the “ny” in “canyon”. ṃ sounds like “ng”. So paññā is said “pan-nyaa” and mettā is said “mettaa”. Hard words. Some English words in this book are hard. The first time a hard word is met in a chapter it has a small number after it, like this: aeons⁵. Its meaning is given at the end of the chapter, under “Hard words in this chapter”, and all the hard words are listed together at the back, after the word list. In the web edition, tapping or clicking on the word shows its meaning. Quizzes. After every two chapters there is a short quiz. Where the stories come from. The stories are not made up. They come from the Jātaka (birth stories) and the Cariyāpiṭaka (Basket of Conduct), two books of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets, the oldest collection of the Buddha’s teaching), and from the old commentaries that explain them. The Buddha told these stories himself. In each one he is the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be), the person who is working, life after life, to become a Buddha. The way they are told here follows the book The Perfections Leading to Enlightenment by Sujin Boriharnwanaket, translated by Nina van Gorkom, which you can read for free on abhidhamma.org when you are older. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 3

Page 4

Introduction: what is a perfection? Imagine a wide, fast river. On this side live all the troubles of the mind: wanting, anger, ignorance1, fear. On the far side there is peace, with none of those troubles. The ancient texts call the far side nibbāna (the end of all troubles). A pāramī (perfection2) is a good quality that carries a person across. That is what the word means: something that goes across to the far shore. This shore kilesa (defilements) wanting anger ignorance Far shore nibbāna (the end of all troubles) peace dāna giving sīla good conduct nekkhamma letting go paññā wisdom viriya energy khanti patience sacca truthfulness adhiṭṭhāna determination mettā loving-kindness upekkhā even mind “the perfections in our daily life as supporting conditions leading to enlightenment” There are ten of them. Here they are, with their Pali names: Pali English What it is in one line dāna giving sharing what one has sīla good conduct not harming by deed3 or word nekkhamma letting go being happy with enough paññā wisdom seeing things as they really are viriya energy4 not being lazy about doing good khanti patience putting up with hard things calmly sacca truthfulness5 being honest in word and deed adhiṭṭhāna determination6 holding firmly to a good aim mettā loving-kindness7 wanting others to be well upekkhā even-mindedness8 staying steady when things go up or down What a person really is. The Abhidhamma (the higher teaching) is the part of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) that explains what the mind really is. It says that what people call a person is really a stream of moments. In each moment there is a citta (consciousness9), a moment of knowing something, and with it some cetasika (mental factors10): feeling, liking, disliking, kindness, laziness and so on. Each citta (consciousness) arises11 because of conditions12, falls away13 at once, and another takes its place. There is The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 4

Page 5

no little person inside who owns them. The ancient texts call this anattā (non-self14). So when this book says that someone gives, or someone is patient, that is only the ordinary way of talking. What is really there is a citta (consciousness) with good cetasika (mental15 factors). Good moments and bad moments. A citta (consciousness) can be kusala (good) or akusala (bad). Every perfection is kusala (good). But not every good deed is a perfection. What makes the difference is the aim behind it. A gift given in the hope of praise, or of being rich in the next life, is still kusala (good). But it is not a perfection. It is a perfection when the danger of wanting, anger and ignorance has been seen, and the aim is to be free of them. The opposite of all ten perfections is lobha (attachment16, wanting). A perfection is good done without wanting anything back. Three roots of trouble. Akusala (bad) states grow from three roots: lobha (attachment), dosa (anger) and moha (ignorance). These three, and the other bad cetasika (mental factors) that grow from them, are called kilesa (defilements17), the things that dirty the mind. All ten perfections work against the kilesa (defilements), until one day they are gone. How each one begins. Each perfection begins when the harm in its opposite is seen. When the harm of stinginess18 is seen, giving arises. When the harm of hurting others is seen, good conduct arises. When the harm of laziness is seen, effort arises. When the harm of impatience is seen, patience arises. When the harm of wanting to get back at people is seen, kindness arises. It is the same for all ten. Medicine for the mind. The road to the far shore is very long. The ancient texts call it the ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga (the noble eightfold path). A sick and weak person cannot walk a long road, even if the way is known. The kilesa (defilements) are the sickness. The ten perfections are the medicine that makes the citta (consciousness) strong enough to walk the whole way. Wishing is not deciding. Some people do a good deed and then pray for a reward. That is a wish, not adhiṭṭhāna (determination). Determination is the firm aim of reaching the far shore and not letting that aim go. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 2. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 3. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 4. energy: effort; the strength that keeps on going 5. truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it 6. determination: making up one's mind firmly and keeping to it 7. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 8. even-mindedness: having a mind that stays level and calm whatever happens 9. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 10. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 11. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 12. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 13. fall away: to end; to stop; to be gone 14. non-self: not a self; not a person; not anyone's 15. mental: to do with the mind 16. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 17. defilement: something that makes the mind dirty: wanting, anger, not knowing and the rest 18. stinginess: not wanting to give or share; meanness The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 5

Page 6

Chapter 1. Dāna (giving) “May I, by this gift, enable beings to achieve long-life, beauty, happiness, strength, intelligence, and the supreme fruit of unsullied bliss.” Dāna (giving) comes first in the list of ten, and there is a reason. A person who cannot let go of a small thing, a sweet or a pencil, will find it much harder to let go of the biggest thing of all: the idea that nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter1) are “me” and “mine”. Giving is practice in letting go. Dāna (giving) What it is letting go of something What it does pushes away greed for things that could be given How it shows itself not holding on tightly What it needs something that can be given away Giving and understanding. Dāna (giving) is giving things away for the good and the happiness of others. At the moment of giving there is no selfishness. The giving can be with paññā (wisdom) or without it. Wisdom at the moment of giving remembers that nothing lasts: not the gift, not the one who gives, not the one who receives. Three kinds of gift. The ancient texts name three kinds of dāna (giving). 1. Āmisa dāna (giving things): food, clothes, money, time, a seat on the bus. 2. Abhaya dāna (giving freedom from fear). When someone decides never to kill any living being2, every creature in the world receives a gift: safety. The same is true of not stealing, not lying, not hurting. The Buddha said that a person who keeps these rules “gives to immeasurable3 beings freedom from fear”. Forgiving is also a gift of this kind: the person who is forgiven is safe from that anger. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 6

Page 7

3. Dhamma dāna (giving the teaching). This is the highest gift. A meal fills a hungry person for a day. Helping someone understand what is really good and really harmful helps them in this life and in the lives to come. āmisa dāna giving things food, clothes, money abhaya dāna giving freedom from fear not killing, not stealing, not lying, not hurting; forgiving dhamma dāna giving the teaching helping another person to right understanding; the highest gift “three kinds of dāna pārami, perfection of generosity: the giving of material things (āmisadāna), the giving of fearlessness (abhayadāna) and the giving of the Dhamma (dhammadāna)” When is giving a perfection? Only when nothing is wanted back. Not praise. Not a present in return. Not even a happy rebirth4 in a deva (heavenly being) world. Giving done in order to look good is still kusala (good), but it is not a perfection5. Only the citta (consciousness6) at the moment of giving shows which it is. How the Bodhisatta gave. The ancient commentary7 tells how the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) gave in his past lives: When he saw that someone needed something, he gave it before they asked. He gave what people wanted, not what they did not want. If there was not enough for everyone, he shared out evenly what there was. He never gave things that harm people: weapons, poison, strong drink. He did not give a sick person food that would make them worse, even if they begged for it. He gave with a smile and kind words, never with a frown. If he gave food, he added clothes. If he gave clothes, he added food. If he noticed greed growing for some beautiful thing of his, he found someone to give the thing to, and gave it away. The four knots. Sometimes there is something to give and someone who needs it, and still the citta (consciousness) does not want to give. The commentary names four knots that tie giving up, and the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) had a thought ready for each one. 1. Not feeling like it. Giving does not come easily now because it was not practised in the past. So he gave anyway, so that in the future the mind would be glad to give. 2. The poor gift. His things were poor now because he had not given in the past. So he gave what he had. 3. The beautiful gift. He had set his heart on the highest goal of all. For that goal it was right to give the loveliest things. 4. Loss. All things get lost and wear out, whether they are given or not. So he gave. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 7

Page 8

That last thought is worth keeping. Fires, floods, thieves and kings take people’s things all the time. Whether a thing is kept or lost depends on kamma (deeds8 and their results9), not on whether it was given. Three moments. Cetanā (intention10) in giving has three moments: before, when the decision to give is made; during, when the gift is handed over; after, when the giving is remembered. The citta (consciousness) can be kusala (good) at all three moments, or it can slip. Someone gives gladly, and afterwards thinks with pride what a generous11 person they are. That afterthought is lobha (attachment12), not giving. So the mind has to be watched. A gift that cannot be held. Can a sound be given? The commentary says it can. A drum can be given to a temple, so that the drum can be beaten. The teaching can be chanted aloud. Gladness at someone else’s good deed can be said out loud. That last one has a name: anumodana (rejoicing13 in another’s good deed). It costs nothing, and it is a gift. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. matter: the kind of reality that does not know or feel anything, such as hardness, colour or sound 2. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 3. immeasurable: too big to measure 4. rebirth: being born again in a new life after this one ends 5. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 6. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 7. commentary: an old explanation of a text, written to make it clear 8. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 9. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 10. intention: what the mind means to do; the mind's choosing 11. generosity: giving freely and gladly 12. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 13. rejoice: to be glad The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 8

Page 9

Chapter 2. Sīla (good conduct) “Sakka, in the guise of a brahmin, came to see the ascetic Akitti” Sīla (good conduct) means not harming anyone by what is done or said. The ancient texts call it tapa (burning away), because good conduct burns away the dirt of akusala (bad states). Sīla (good conduct) What it is keeping deeds1 and words in order What it does drives out bad behaviour How it shows itself a clean way of living What it needs hiri (shame at doing wrong) and ottappa (fear of the results2 of doing wrong) The five rules. The most basic sīla (good conduct) is the pañca sīla (five precepts3): 1. not to kill any living being4 2. not to take what is not given 3. not to do wrong in sexual matters 4. not to lie 5. not to drink or take anything that clouds the mind When one of these rules is broken, the citta (consciousness5) behind it is always akusala (bad). At that moment there is no mettā (loving-kindness6) for the one being harmed. A sotāpanna (stream-enterer, a person who has reached the first stage of enlightenment7) keeps all five rules perfectly and can never break them again. Nobody else can promise that. But the rules can still be kept, moment by moment, long before that stage is reached. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 9

Page 10

Two kinds of shame. Two cetasika (mental factors8) are the nearest cause of good conduct. Hiri (shame) comes from inside: its nearest cause is respect for oneself. Ottappa (fear of blame) comes from outside: its nearest cause is respect for someone else. The two always arise9 together, and both keep the rules. If a person breaks a rule by forgetting, shame or fear of blame makes him quickly put it right. The story of Akitti. Long ago the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was an ascetic10 named Akitti. He lived alone in a forest beside a great Kāra tree. When the tree had fruit, he ate the fruit. When it had none, he ate its leaves, boiled in water, and he gathered only enough for one meal a day. the great Kāra tree his hermitage sodden Kāra leaves Akitti the brahmin Sakka in disguise “If the ascetic Akitti wishes to become Sakka, he will give me his sodden Kāra leaves, but if he has not such a wish, he will not give them away.” Sakka, the king of the devas (heavenly beings), saw this pure and simple life and wondered what Akitti wanted. Perhaps he wanted to become Sakka himself? So Sakka came down disguised as a brahmin11 (a priest) and stood before the hut as if asking for food. Akitti saw that the brahmin needed food. He gave him all the leaves. The next day the brahmin came again, and Akitti gave him all the leaves again. The third day, the same. Sakka saw that this was no bargain for heaven. It was dāna (giving) with sīla (good conduct), nekkhamma (letting go), khanti (patience), viriya (energy12), adhiṭṭhāna (determination13) and sacca (truthfulness14) all at once, with no wish for anything back. In each of his lives the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) developed all ten perfections15 together. Sakka showed himself and asked why Akitti lived there alone. Akitti answered: “Sakka, King of the devas, rebirth16 is dukkha, the breaking up of the body is dukkha, and dying with delusion17 is dukkha. Therefore I dwell here all alone.” Dukkha (suffering18) is the way everything that arises never quite satisfies. Sakka was pleased and offered him any wish he liked. Akitti asked, one wish at a time: 1. To be free from all attachment19, even the harmless kind that people feel for their children and their things. 2. That there be no akusala kamma (bad deed) that could make him lose land, goods, cattle or relatives. 3. Not to see, hear or sit with fools, because fools advise what is wrong and answer good advice with anger. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 10

Page 11

4. That people see the wise and listen to them, because the wise advise what is right. 5. That holy beggars might come to his hut each morning, that the food he offered them never run out, and that he never regret his giving. 6. That Sakka never visit him again. That last wish surprised Sakka. Most people long to see a deva (heavenly being). Akitti explained that devas (heavenly beings) are glorious and delightful to look at, and seeing them might make him break his vow. Sakka agreed, and left. Akitti lived in that place all his life and was reborn in the brahma (highest heavenly) world. The Buddha said that Sakka in that story was Anuruddha, one of his great disciples20, and Akitti was himself. Jotipāla and the bad friends. Akitti stayed away from fools, and the next story shows why. In another life the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was a young brahmin (priest) called Jotipāla. His family had no faith in the Buddha of that age, the Buddha Kassapa, and Jotipāla copied his parents and looked down on the Buddha too. The commentary21 says that all the perfections Jotipāla had gathered over so many lives were like a bright blazing fire. In that life the fire met water: the fire went out, and only black charcoal was left. Bad company can do that even to a Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be). The commentary compares the company of fools to drinking bitter water, and the company of the wise to drinking sweet water. a bright blazing fire the perfections gathered over many lives water bad friends and wrong views black charcoal the light was gone “the rays of light disappeared and only black charcoal was left” Two sides of good conduct. Vāritta sīla (conduct as avoiding) is not doing wrong: the five rules. Cāritta sīla (conduct as doing) is doing what is right. The commentary lists what the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-tobe) did. He greeted good people with respect. He looked after them when they were ill. He put up with insults from unkind people. He remembered every kindness done to him. When he did wrong, he admitted it. He guided the blind and found a cart for those who could not walk. He hid his own good qualities and admitted his faults. And when he heard about the great deeds of Bodhisattas (Buddhas-to-be) of the past, he was not frightened off. They were only human beings, who trained step by step, and the same training would bring him to the same goal. Good conduct right now. A dear friend does something wrong, and without thinking a person scolds the friend in front of everyone. When sati (mindfulness22, remembering what is good) arises instead, the scolding waits, and the friend is spoken to later, kindly and alone. The kilesa (defilements23) have to be worn away like that, again and again. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. deed: something done; an act, good or bad The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 11

Page 12

2. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 3. precept: a rule of good conduct 4. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 5. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 6. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 7. enlightenment: the moment when the truth is seen fully and for good, and the dirt of the mind is cut away 8. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 9. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 10. ascetic: a person who gives up home and comfort to live simply and seek the truth; or that hard way of living 11. brahmin: a man of the priestly class in ancient India 12. energy: effort; the strength that keeps on going 13. determination: making up one's mind firmly and keeping to it 14. truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it 15. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 16. rebirth: being born again in a new life after this one ends 17. delusion: being fooled; not seeing things as they are 18. suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give lasting happiness 19. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 20. disciple: a pupil; someone who follows a teacher 21. commentary: an old explanation of a text, written to make it clear 22. mindfulness: noticing what is really there right now, without forgetting 23. defilement: something that makes the mind dirty: wanting, anger, not knowing and the rest The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 12

Page 13

Quiz 1 (chapters 1 and 2) The answers are at the back. 1. What does the word pāramī (perfection) mean? (a) a gift for a king (b) a quality that crosses over to the further shore, the eradication of defilements (c) a kind of prayer (d) a letter of the Pali alphabet 2. The book says the ten perfections have one thing as their opposite. What is it? (a) dosa (aversion) (b) lobha (attachment) (c) sati (mindfulness) (d) paññā (wisdom) 3. The Buddha said that a noble disciple who gives up the taking of life gives something to immeasurable beings. What does he give them? (a) food and drink (b) freedom from fear, freedom from hostility and freedom from oppression (c) gold and silver (d) a long life 4. Which of these does the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) not give? (a) what is needed, to whoever stands in need of it, even unasked (b) an excellent and beautiful object (c) weapons, poisons and intoxicants (d) a gift together with a bonus 5. When the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) is giving a gift and sees the loss of the object being given, what does he reflect, and what does he then do? 6. Finish the sentence from the book: “No matter how much we give away, generosity is not a perfection if we do not see the need to …” 7. In the story of Akitti, in what guise did Sakka come, what did Akitti give him, and for how many days? 8. Why did Akitti ask Sakka not to visit him again? 9. Hiri (shame) and ottappa (fear of blame) are the nearest cause of sīla (good conduct). Which one has respect for oneself as its cause, and which one respect for someone else? 10. True or false: a sotāpanna (stream-enterer) can still transgress the five precepts now and then. 11. What does the commentary compare the perfections of young Jotipāla to, in the life when he was born among people of wrong view? The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 13

Page 14

Chapter 3. Nekkhamma (letting go) “Since my older brother Sona did not accept your possessions, I will not accept them either” Nekkhamma (letting go) is turning away from the chase after pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches. Most people think it means becoming a monk1. The ancient texts say it can begin at home, at the moment someone looks at what they have and finds it is enough. Nekkhamma (letting go) What it is moving away from sense pleasures What it does shows that they never quite satisfy How it shows itself drawing back from them What it needs saṃvega (a sense of urgency2, a jolt that says life is short) Three kinds of thinking. The ancient texts name three wrong ways of thinking: kāma vitakka (thinking about sense pleasures), vyāpāda vitakka (thinking with hate) and vihiṃsā vitakka (thinking about hurting). The opposite of the first is nekkhamma vitakka (thinking of letting go). When the mind wants more pleasant things than it already has, that is kāma vitakka (thinking about sense pleasures). When the mind finds that what it has is enough, that is nekkhamma vitakka (thinking of letting go). A person who stops buying more clothes just to look nice, and gives the spare ones to someone who can use them, has nekkhamma (letting go) in daily life. Monk or not. A monk who still clings3 to pleasant things just as a layperson4 does is, in that way, no different from a layperson. And a layperson who clings less is practising nekkhamma (letting go) without a robe. Clinging to the five sense objects5 is not fully gone until a person becomes an anāgāmī (non-returner, the third stage of enlightenment6). Until then, the work is to make the clinging smaller, bit by bit. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 14

Page 15

The story of Sona and Nanda. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was once born as Sona, the son of a very rich brahmin7 (priest). His little brother was Nanda, who in a later life became the Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha’s attendant. Their parents wanted them to marry. Sona would not. He wanted to look after his parents all their lives and then become an ascetic8 (a person who gives up home and comfort to train the mind). Nanda said that he would do the same. Then the parents decided to go with them. All four left home and built a hut in the forest, and the two brothers cared for their parents. Nanda's fruit gathered the day before: some spoilt, some unripe Sona's fruit sweet and ripe, gathered further away “Nanda brings all kinds of half-ripe or unripe fruits for them to eat and therefore they will not live long.” Nanda gathered fruit the day before and served it early in the morning. But fruit kept from the day before was sometimes spoilt or unripe. Sona went further into the forest for sweet ripe fruit, but by the time he came back the parents had already eaten Nanda’s fruit. Sona was worried: the parents were old, and bad fruit would shorten their lives. He told Nanda to wait each day until he came back, so that both could serve the parents together. Nanda did not listen. He wanted the merit9 of feeding the parents to be his own. So Sona sent him away. Nanda went off alone and developed deep calm of mind and the higher powers. Then he wanted to ask his brother’s forgiveness, in the grandest way he could. He thought of bringing Sakka, the king of the devas (heavenly beings10), but decided that was not fitting. Instead he brought the mightiest king on earth, King Manoja. So the king came to the hut, and Nanda was forgiven. From then on Nanda looked after their mother and Sona looked after their father. Then Sona taught the king about caring for one’s parents: Joy, careless ease, laughter and sport, are the sure heritage Of him that studiously11 shall tend a mother in old age. Where is the nekkhamma (letting go) in this story? Sona gave up a fortune and a wedding, paid no attention to sense pleasures, and used every spare moment to develop jhāna (deep calm of mind). Letting go in small things. Three everyday examples. Pictures. Something beautiful is seen and enjoyed. If sati (mindfulness12) arises13, it is known that this is only a dhamma (a reality14) appearing. When the beautiful thing is not there, it is not searched for. Food. A person is full, but the food is delicious, so one more mouthful goes in. That is the citta (consciousness15) clinging to taste. Eating just enough to feed the body is nekkhamma (letting go). The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 15
